what: BRP, based in Quebec, makes powersports vehicles: Ski-Doo and Lynx snowmobiles, Sea-Doo personal watercraft, Can-Am off-road side-by-sides and ATVs, Can-Am three-wheeled motorcycles, and Rotax engines. In 2025 it sold its boat businesses to focus on these core lines.
customers: Recreational riders and outdoor enthusiasts in North America, Europe and elsewhere, buying through a network of independent dealers that also stock BRP parts and accessories.
money: Can-Am side-by-sides, ATVs and three-wheelers, sold in every season.
Ski-Doo and Lynx snowmobiles and Sea-Doo personal watercraft.
Higher-margin aftermarket sales to the installed base of vehicles.
moat: BRP leads or co-leads every category it competes in: Ski-Doo and Sea-Doo are the best-selling brands in snowmobiles and personal watercraft, and Can-Am has taken share in side-by-sides from Polaris. Its own Rotax engines, a large dealer network and a parts business tied to millions of vehicles in use give it scale advantages that smaller rivals cannot match.
risks: Equity of only $231M against $2.1B of debt, the result of years of buybacks, leaves little cushion in a downturn.
Powersports are discretionary purchases often financed with credit, so higher interest rates hit demand.
Dealer inventories swelled in 2024 and forced production cuts; destocking can return.
Revenue fell from $7.46B in fiscal 2023 to $5.46B in fiscal 2025 before recovering.
US tariffs on Canadian and Mexican-made vehicles could raise costs.
opportunities: The shares trade at about 15.9 times forward earnings and 5.3 times free cash flow.
Free cash flow of $838M over the last twelve months against a $4.4B market value is a yield near 19%.
Analysts expect earnings per share to rise about 30% next year as volumes recover from the destocking trough.
Selling the marine business removed a loss-making division and simplifies the company.
Market share gains in side-by-sides against Polaris continue.
watch: Retail sales versus wholesale shipments. When dealers sell more to riders than BRP ships to dealers, inventory is clean and the next leg of growth is coming.
view: BRP is the best operator in powersports and has the market share to prove it: Ski-Doo and Sea-Doo dominate their categories, and Can-Am has spent a decade taking side-by-side share from Polaris. The past two years have been a test of that quality. Dealers overstocked after the pandemic boom, rates rose, and BRP cut production, sending revenue from $7.46 billion in fiscal 2023 to $5.46 billion in fiscal 2025 and producing a small loss that year. The 58 times trailing P/E reflects that trough, not the business.

The recovery has started. Revenue has climbed back to about $6.6 billion over the last twelve months, free cash flow was $838 million, and the sale of the money-losing boat business removed a distraction. The concern is the balance sheet: years of aggressive buybacks have left shareholders’ equity at just $231 million against $2.1 billion of debt. That is fine when free cash flow is this strong and dangerous when it is not, which makes BRP more cyclical than its brands suggest.

The market prices BRP somewhere between a trough and a recovery, about 15.9 times forward earnings with analysts expecting a 30% rise in earnings per share next year. I think that is reasonable value for the leader in its industry, provided the consumer holds up. The one thing it turns on is retail demand: if riders keep buying at current levels while dealer inventory stays lean, the earnings recovery is conservative; if higher rates and a weaker economy hit discretionary spending, the thin equity cushion makes the downside steeper than at Polaris.
bull: Retail demand holds, dealer inventories stay lean, earnings recover about 30%, and a near-19% free cash flow yield drives the shares higher.
bear: Rates and a weaker consumer hit powersports demand, destocking returns, and BRP’s thin equity cushion magnifies the downturn.
